planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby; Ennis is susceptible to eastern filbert blight and best suited to the drier Pacific Northwest growing region.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby; Ennis is susceptible to eastern filbert blight and best suited to the drier Pacific Northwest growing region. A classic Oregon hazelnut cultivar prized for producing exceptionally large, high-quality kernels favored by the fresh-eating and confectionery trade, it has long been a benchmark large-nut variety even as newer blight-resistant cultivars have gained ground in commercial orchards. Like older Pacific Northwest hazelnut cultivars bred before eastern filbert blight resistance was a priority, it is quite susceptible to that serious fungal disease and performs best in the relatively dry summer climate of western Oregon, struggling with disease pressure in humid eastern growing regions. Plant a compatible pollinator variety within range for good nut set, and monitor closely for filbert blight cankers, pruning out infected wood promptly if the disease appears.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Beaumont macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, but bears at a younger age than many macadamia cultivars.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Beaumont macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, but bears at a younger age than many macadamia cultivars. A hybrid between the two main macadamia species, this Australian-bred cultivar is widely planted for home gardens and smaller orchards because it begins bearing noticeably earlier than many other macadamia selections, often within three to four years, and produces large clusters of good-quality nuts on a moderately vigorous tree. Its relatively quick time to first bearing makes it a popular choice for home growers wanting a faster return than the decade-plus wait typical of some macadamia cultivars, though like all macadamias it needs consistent warmth and is easily damaged by frost. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and harvest nuts as they fall naturally from the tree when fully mature, since immature nuts do not ripen further once picked.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Own Choice macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued for its naturally compact, easy-care habit.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Own Choice macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued for its naturally compact, easy-care habit. This Australian-bred cultivar is prized for a naturally more compact, self-shaping growth habit that needs little pruning to maintain a manageable size compared to larger, more sprawling macadamia varieties, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or smaller property with limited space. It produces reliable crops of good-quality, high-oil-content nuts and, like other named macadamia cultivars, benefits from cross-pollination with a second variety planted nearby to maximize nut set. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and allow nuts to fall naturally from the tree at full maturity before collecting and drying them for storage or cracking.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; A4 macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued commercially for high oil content and cracking quality.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; A4 macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued commercially for high oil content and cracking quality. One of the classic Hawaiian-selected macadamia cultivars developed for commercial orchards, it produces medium-sized nuts with a high proportion of premium-grade, whole-kernel cracking quality and rich, high oil content prized by processors, making it a benchmark variety in Hawaiian macadamia production for decades. Like other macadamias it needs consistent warmth, protection from frost, and several years of growth before reaching significant bearing age, along with a compatible cross-pollinator variety for the best nut set. Water regularly during nut development, allow nuts to mature and fall naturally before harvest, and provide the same warm, humid, frost-free conditions the species requires throughout the year.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Barbara macadamia is somewhat more cold-tolerant than Macadamia integrifolia cultivars but still needs a largely frost-free climate to thrive.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Barbara macadamia is somewhat more cold-tolerant than Macadamia integrifolia cultivars but still needs a largely frost-free climate to thrive. A rough-shelled macadamia cultivar selected in coastal California, it belongs to the Macadamia tetraphylla species, which is generally hardier and better suited to California's cooler coastal climate than the smooth-shelled Macadamia integrifolia cultivars more commonly grown in Hawaii and Australia, producing flavorful, high-quality nuts with a thicker, more difficult-to-crack shell. Its improved cold tolerance relative to other macadamia species has made tetraphylla cultivars like this one the more practical choice for California growers outside the warmest coastal microclimates. Water regularly during nut development, provide the most sheltered, frost-free site available, and allow nuts to mature and fall naturally before harvest and shelling.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; shagbark hickory develops a long taproot and transplants best while young and dormant, with minimal root disturbance.

directions: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; shagbark hickory develops a long taproot and transplants best while young and dormant, with minimal root disturbance. A named selection prized among nut tree enthusiasts for producing thinner-shelled, easier-to-crack nuts with excellent sweet flavor compared to typical wild shagbark hickory seedlings, which often have very thick, difficult shells that discourage home processing despite the excellent nut quality. Like all shagbark hickories it is a large, long-lived forest tree distinguished by its shaggy, peeling bark and needs considerable time, often a decade or more, before reaching significant nut-bearing maturity, making it a true multi-generational planting. Provide deep, well-drained soil and full sun, protect the young tree's long taproot from damage during transplanting, and be prepared for a long wait before the improved, easier-cracking nuts this selection is known for become available in quantity.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
